idiom_name: readonly snapshot interfaces + ReadonlyArray history with findLast / indexed lookup
implementation_notes: The version is an interface whose fields are all readonly and the history is typed ReadonlyArray<Version>, so the compiler rejects the in-place edit that would rewrite history while a change is expressed as a spread copy carrying a new effective date. The continuity is a class or an object carrying the identity plus that history; as-of is findLast(v => v.effective <= on) for short histories, or a binary search over a readonly number[] of epoch milliseconds when history is long. TypeScript adds no runtime versioning, so the structure matches the JavaScript realization - what it adds is the type-level guarantee that published versions cannot be assigned to, plus discriminated unions for typing published versions against proposed amendments.
pitfalls: readonly is compile-time only and erased in the emitted JavaScript, so runtime mutation through a cast or parsed JSON still needs Object.freeze at the boundary.
readonly is shallow: Readonly<Version> does not make a nested terms object readonly - use nested readonly interfaces and ReadonlyArray deliberately.
Array.prototype.findLast is ES2023: with an older lib target it is a type error and in old engines a runtime absence, so an explicit reverse loop or an epoch-millisecond index avoids the dependency.
Timestamps compared as strings ('2024-03-01') sort correctly only while zero-padded and timezone-free; mixing string and numeric effective dates in one history makes every comparison silently wrong.
